Pregnancy

Vaginal changes during pregnancy and after birth

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy changes the vagina, the external vulva and the pelvic floor as well as the abdomen and breasts. More discharge, fullness or altered sensation can occur, but a symptom should not be dismissed simply because you are pregnant or have recently given birth. Knowing your usual pattern helps you explain a change; it does not replace maternity assessment for bleeding, possible leaking waters or illness.

Which parts change, and why?

The vagina is the internal canal; the vulva includes the labia and skin around its opening. The perineum is between the vaginal opening and anus. Hormonal changes and increased pelvic blood flow can affect moisture, tissue fullness and colour during pregnancy. The vulva or vaginal entrance may look darker or bluish. Appearance varies and does not confirm pregnancy or tell you whether the pregnancy is healthy.

Some people notice increased sensitivity or sexual arousal, while others have less desire, discomfort or no change. Swelling does not mean you should want sex. New persistent symptoms, a painful lump, sores, marked redness or sudden severe swelling deserve clinical assessment rather than being labelled a normal hormonal change.

More discharge: common, but not every leak is discharge

Healthy pregnancy discharge is often thin, clear or milky white without an unpleasant smell, and the amount may increase. A mild natural scent is different from a new bad smell. Comfortable underwear and frequent changes of damp clothing may help. If a liner is needed, choose an unscented one and stop if it irritates; do not try to eliminate normal discharge with internal washing.

Ask your midwife about changed smell, yellow or green discharge, itching, soreness or pain when passing urine. A watery trickle or gush could be urine, discharge or amniotic fluid: colour and smell at home cannot reliably distinguish them. If you suspect your waters are leaking at any stage of pregnancy, contact maternity immediately, even without pain. A pad, not a tampon, can help you record the fluid while seeking advice; do not wait for a home test to confirm it.

Thrush, bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis

Thrush is a yeast infection that may cause itching, soreness and thick white discharge, usually without a strong smell. Pregnancy can make it more common, but symptoms alone do not prove yeast and it is unhelpful to promise that any vaginal symptom has zero effect on a baby. Seek advice before treatment. CDC guidance recommends a seven-day topical azole for vaginal thrush in pregnancy rather than oral fluconazole; yoghurt and probiotics are not substitutes.

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a bacterial imbalance, not a fungal infection; thin discharge and a fishy smell can occur. Symptomatic BV in pregnancy should be assessed and treated, as it is associated with complications including preterm birth and early membrane rupture, without meaning these will happen to you. Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause odorous discharge, irritation or urinary pain and is also associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes. Testing distinguishes causes; symptomatic pregnant patients need treatment, and current partners need treatment for trichomoniasis. Wait to have sex until you and your partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Ask about repeat testing and diagnosis-specific partner advice; do not share medicines or assume one cream treats every infection.

Swelling, colour and symptoms needing assessment

Gradual vulvar fullness can accompany increased blood flow, but infection, irritation, a cyst or a vein problem can also cause swelling. Contact your maternity clinician for swelling with redness, itching, burning, discharge or a new painful area. A rapidly enlarging or very painful one-sided swelling, particularly after birth, needs urgent assessment; severe pain, faintness or heavy bleeding requires immediate emergency care.

Do not squeeze a lump, insert a treatment for an assumed infection or continue painful sex. An examination, with your consent, and selected swabs or urine tests may be needed. You can ask for a chaperone and for the examination to stop. Darkening or visible veins alone cannot establish the cause of a painful change.

Vulvar varicose veins and comfort

Vulvar varicosities are enlarged veins on the external genitals. Pregnancy-related blood-flow changes and slower venous return can cause pooling, pressure, fullness or a bluish, bumpy appearance. Symptoms may worsen after prolonged standing, activity or sex. A clinician can check that a lump or pain is actually a vein problem; not every swelling is a varicosity.

Changing position, avoiding long periods standing or sitting, a wrapped cool compress and an appropriately fitted support garment may help. Ask your maternity team about comfortable rest positions and leg support rather than routinely lying flat on your back to raise your hips in later pregnancy. These veins often improve after birth, but there is no guaranteed deadline. They usually do not prevent vaginal birth; a personalised birth plan and review of severe or persistent symptoms are appropriate.

Bleeding during pregnancy: get advice about the symptom

Contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service immediately for any vaginal bleeding, including spotting without pain. Do not decide it is implantation bleeding from its timing or colour. Causes range from cervical changes or infection to miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or placental problems. Later bleeding may also accompany preterm labour, early cervical opening, placental separation or, rarely, uterine rupture; you do not need to know which cause applies before seeking help.

Heavy bleeding that quickly soaks a pad, severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care. Near term, a small amount of blood-streaked jelly-like mucus can be a show as the cervix changes, but fresh or greater bleeding should not be dismissed as a show. Suspected labour before 37 weeks, reduced baby movements or leaking waters needs immediate maternity contact, not waiting until the next day. Pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or hurts with movement or touch also needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Soreness, bruising and stitches after birth

After vaginal birth, stretching, bruising and swelling may make the perineum sore, and urination or bowel movements may be uncomfortable. Tears or an episiotomy can need repair and a specific recovery plan. Not everyone has the same injury or symptoms; a caesarean birth does not remove the need to assess vaginal bleeding or pelvic symptoms. Healing varies and is not guaranteed by a six-week date.

Follow your team's wound-care and pain-relief advice, including checking medicines when breastfeeding. Gentle external rinsing, patting dry, changing pads and avoiding constipation can help. Do not put ice directly on skin. Increasing pain or swelling, pus, an opening wound, bad smell or fever needs prompt clinical advice; fever with worsening abdominal pain or feeling unwell needs urgent help now. Severe rapidly increasing pain or swelling, faintness or heavy bleeding needs emergency care.

Postpartum bleeding: lochia versus a warning sign

Lochia is bleeding and discharge from the uterus after birth, including after a caesarean. It generally reduces and changes colour over several weeks; duration varies. This does not make heavy bright-red bleeding with clots automatically normal in the first 24 hours or at any later time. Tell the maternity team about increasing bleeding, clots or a pattern that worries you; do not judge safety only by the number of days since birth.

Sudden or very heavy bleeding, soaking one or more pads in an hour, large clots or tissue needs immediate medical assessment; call emergency services for very heavy bleeding, faintness, dizziness, a pounding heart, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty. Do not wait to reach a pad count if bleeding is severe or you feel unwell. Bad-smelling discharge, fever or increasing lower abdominal pain needs urgent advice now. Use maternity or period pads while healing; avoid tampons and menstrual cups until your team confirms it is appropriate, commonly after the postnatal check. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Pelvic floor recovery is individual

Pregnancy and birth can change pelvic support, bladder control and how the vagina feels. A stretched feeling does not define your worth or guarantee permanent dysfunction. Pelvic floor muscle training can help prevent or manage some symptoms, but it cannot promise that every vagina returns to a previous shape or that prolapse will never occur.

Ask a trained clinician or pelvic health physiotherapist to help with correct contraction and full relaxation, tailored to your ability, pain and goals. Do not simply add more forceful Kegels when they hurt. Persistent leaking, a vaginal bulge or heaviness, bowel-control problems or pain deserves assessment and support; you do not have to wait for a routine check if it troubles you. Recovery and return to exercise follow your symptoms and birth injuries.

Dryness, intimacy and contraception

Lower oestrogen after birth, particularly during breastfeeding, can contribute to dryness, burning or uncomfortable penetration. A water-based lubricant may help; ask about an appropriate vaginal moisturiser or prescribed treatment if symptoms persist. Do not assume that a product labelled natural is safe for healing tissue. Oil-based products can weaken latex condoms, so check compatibility.

There is no universal date for resuming sex. Consent, comfort, healing, bleeding and any specific clinical restrictions matter; stop if it hurts and seek help for persistent pain or bleeding. Closeness does not require penetration, and no one owes sexual activity during recovery. Pregnancy can occur from around three weeks after birth, before a period returns and while breastfeeding. Arrange suitable contraception with your clinician rather than relying on dryness, breastfeeding alone or an app.

Everyday care without unnecessary products

Wash the vulva gently with your hands and lukewarm water, then pat dry; you do not need a hair dryer. Keep cleansing external and avoid douching, scented pads, wipes, sprays, perfumes and antiseptics. Irritated skin may need a clinician-recommended fragrance-free soap substitute. Wipe from front to back, choose comfortable clothes and change damp underwear. These steps support comfort rather than guarantee prevention of infection.

A varied diet, ordinary hydration, fibre to help prevent constipation and suitable activity support general recovery. Eating yoghurt or cutting sugar is not a proven vaginal infection treatment, and symptoms are not a reason to blame your food choices. Follow pregnancy food-safety guidance. For a worrying change, contact your care team instead of adding a probiotic, pH product or home remedy. BeMama can help organise symptom notes and appointment questions, but cannot assess bleeding, diagnose infection or leaking waters, or certify healing.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Contact your maternity team immediately for any pregnancy bleeding, possible leaking waters, reduced baby movements or possible labour before 37 weeks. Describe the timing and symptoms; do not wait to identify the cause or for an app to reassure you.

Ask a clinician to assess new painful swelling, changed discharge, itching or urinary pain before choosing treatment. Follow the diagnosis-specific pregnancy treatment and partner advice; do not insert foods, douche or assume an antifungal treats every cause.

Follow your individual wound-care and pelvic-floor plan, including full muscle relaxation; ask for help if pain, leakage or a bulge persists. Resume intimacy only with consent and comfort, discuss contraception, and seek emergency help for warning signs rather than waiting for a six-week check.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record changes, their timing and questions for your maternity or postnatal appointment. It cannot diagnose infection or leaking waters, assess blood loss or wound healing, exclude an emergency, or replace your care team's advice. Contact clinical services for warning signs regardless of what an app records.

When to seek help

Contact maternity immediately for any pregnancy bleeding and for suspected leaking waters, reduced movements or possible labour before 37 weeks. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder pain, faintness or loss of consciousness needs emergency care now. After birth, severe bleeding or bleeding with dizziness, a pounding heart or breathlessness needs emergency services; large clots or soaking a pad in an hour needs immediate assessment. Fever, bad-smelling discharge, worsening abdominal or wound pain needs urgent advice now. Do not wait for a routine visit or an app to reassure you. Pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or hurts with movement or touch also needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • More discharge and gradual vulvar fullness or colour changes can occur; a painful or persistent change still needs assessment.
  • Any pregnancy bleeding needs immediate maternity contact. Suspected leaking waters, reduced movements or preterm labour signs need immediate maternity contact.
  • Heavy postpartum bleeding is not automatically normal in the first day. Severe bleeding or faintness needs emergency help, and fever, bad smell or worsening pain needs urgent assessment.
  • Infection treatment, wound care, pelvic floor exercises and return to sex should fit your diagnosis and recovery. Avoid internal cleaning and unproven food or product cures.

Frequently asked questions

What does normal pregnancy discharge look like?

It is often thin, clear or milky white without an unpleasant smell and may increase. Colour alone cannot confirm that everything is well. Ask about changed smell, itching, pain or unusual colour; contact maternity immediately for possible leaking waters or any pregnancy bleeding.

When is swelling not a routine pregnancy change?

Swelling with redness, burning, itching, unusual discharge or a painful lump needs clinical assessment. Rapidly enlarging or very painful swelling needs urgent help; severe pain, heavy bleeding, faintness, fainting or loss of consciousness each needs emergency care. Do not squeeze it or assume it is an infection. Pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or hurts with movement or touch also needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Can pregnancy make the vulva fuller or darker?

Yes. Increased blood flow and hormonal changes can cause fullness and darker or bluish colour. Sensitivity and desire vary, and swelling does not require sexual activity. Appearance alone cannot confirm pregnancy or explain a new painful change.

Is bruising or soreness after vaginal birth expected?

Some bruising, swelling and soreness can follow stretching, a tear or an episiotomy, with variable healing. Increasing or severe pain, growing swelling, pus, bad smell, fever or wound opening should be assessed. Heavy bleeding or faintness needs emergency help; do not wait six weeks for review.

Can I tell leaking waters from discharge at home?

Not reliably from colour, smell or a home test. If you suspect a watery trickle or gush is amniotic fluid, contact maternity immediately at any gestation. Use a pad rather than a tampon to note fluid while arranging care, without delaying the call.

Is heavy bleeding with clots normal just after birth?

Do not automatically treat it as normal, even in the first 24 hours. Sudden or very heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour, large clots or tissue needs immediate assessment. Severe bleeding, faintness, dizziness, a pounding heart, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs emergency services. Seek help before any threshold if you feel unwell. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Should everyone do more Kegels to recover?

Pelvic floor training can help, but it should include correct relaxation and be tailored to symptoms and injury. Pain, persistent leakage, bowel-control problems or a vaginal bulge warrants assessment and possibly specialist physiotherapy. More forceful squeezing is not a universal solution.

Do yoghurt, less sugar or special washes prevent infection?

They do not provide a proven guarantee or replace diagnosis and treatment. Maintain a balanced diet and safe food choices in pregnancy; do not insert foods or wash inside the vagina. Seek advice for symptoms before choosing antifungals or other products, because pregnancy changes which treatments are appropriate.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
